processing: Not a processed tea at all: fresh tea leaves are mixed with fruit juice, sour bamboo shoots, sour ants, garlic and salt, and eaten.
harvest_season: Made with freshly picked leaves when the plants are flushing; little is documented about a set season.
appearance_dry: There is no dry form: this is a dish of fresh green tea leaves.
appearance_liquor: No brewed liquor; any liquid is a thin, cloudy green dressing from the leaves and seasonings.
appearance_wet: Fresh green leaf, mixed through with pale shreds of bamboo shoot and seasonings.
taste_profile: Given its ingredients, expect sour, salty and garlicky seasoning over the raw bitterness of fresh leaf; little is written about its taste in detail.

brewing.notes: The numbers are placeholders only: this is eaten, not brewed, and no fixed proportions are documented. Mix fresh leaf with the seasonings and serve right away.

vintage_note: It has no vintages and is made from fresh leaf rather than sold as an aged or packaged tea. If you meet it, it will be on Jinuo Mountain or at a Jinuo table.
description:
This is tea as food. The Jinuo people of Jinuo Mountain in Xishuangbanna make a cold dish from fresh tea leaves, known locally as 腊攸, glossed as cold-mixed tea.

One recorded recipe is short: fresh leaves stirred together with fruit juice, sour bamboo shoots, sour ants, garlic and salt. Proportions are not fixed in anything written down, and they probably vary by household.

The taste follows from what goes in: sourness and salt against the bitter green edge of raw leaf. Treat it as a salad rather than a cup, and do not expect any steeps.

It is a dish of fresh leaf rather than a packaged tea, so look for it locally rather than in a tea shop.
history:
Jinuo Mountain is one of the old six pu-erh tea mountains, and the Jinuo have kept up eating fresh tea alongside drinking it. One expert view holds that dishes like this may lie behind the tea foods once eaten in Han areas, but that is a suggestion rather than a documented line.

A tea culture event in Jinuo Township in Jinghong has featured it as a Jinuo technique. Beyond that, little is documented about its age or how it has changed.
